c4c436c5be8c11c0ccefa8e7b937edb5d98c4d1c.message:
make PreparedQuery Sendable

I'm using this package for incoming request authorization in a few
different network services. A pattern I've been trying out is to build a
`PreparedQuery` on startup, attach it to my server handler class/struct,
and call `evaluate` on it for every request. In the HTTP/gRPC frameworks
I've been using, these server handler objects have to be `Sendable`, and
the easiest way to do so is to make sure all the properties are
`Sendable` too.

Right now, as all the implementations of `Evaluator` and `Store`, and
`PreparedQuery` itself are all value types, making them conform to
`Sendable` was just a matter of bookkeeping. But, assuming API stability
is important, this is making an important change. We're signing up for
all future implementations of `Store` to be `Sendable`, and
`PreparedQuery` to remain so for all time.

Eventually, especially as use cases arise for patching a `Store` after
it's been initialized and prepared for a query, I don't think
`InMemoryStore` should stay a value type. But, just for conformance's
sake now, I think it's fine to keep it and accept that it adds costs for
copying potential large data sets to transport across concurrency
domains.

Signed-off-by: Chris Rice <chrisrice@apple.com>

* prepareForEval->prepareForEvaluation
* RegoValue patch/merge, RegoEncodingError -> package visibility
* integrate functiondecl code from capabilities branch
* rename swift-rego -> swift-opa

* remove unused Runtime module
* public -> internal CodingKeys
* update README.md

* Manifest -> OPA.Manifest
* add documentation tags for some top-level types

196b102d199fa0fb18b5cee015df9047ec579b65.message:
Support strict builtin errors (#61)

The general pattern being that builtins throw errors when something
is wrong (invalid args, some undefined behavior, failures, etc) and
it is up to the caller to decide out whether or not to propagate the
error.

This introduces a new `BuiltinErrors.halt` flavor of error which, when
thrown, will _always_ propagate and stop the evaluation. These are
to be used for operations that signify something seriously wrong and
the policy evaluation should not continue. This concept is the same in
OPA's topdown evaluator and builtin definitions. It seems only a few
builtins use it, but it does get used in some places. So far it does
not appear that we have any implemented which need it.

Signed-off-by: Patrick East <p_east@apple.com>

Example:

```

```

`x` is determined at runtime, and may or may not map to a function called `data.policy.dynamic.<package-x>.deny`.

ffce6a8e485126662324372dfa1d5164bb3ee5b5.message:
perf: wrap statements in AnyStatement enum for up to 2x performance boost ⚡️ (#39)

During decoding, we now wrap concrete statement structs in a new
AnyStatement enum. This allows our core evaluation loop in evalBlock to
dispatch in O(1) rather than O(number of possible statements), which in
practice gives us up to a 2x measured performance increase.

Previously, profiling showed swift_dynamicCast in the hot path as the
switch enumerated over each potential concrete statement type.

> Enums are designed so that we can easily recover an index for the
> case, so a simple switch over an enum can be compiled by finding this
> index and then using a standard switch-over-restricted-int pattern, such
> as a local dispatch table.

Signed-off-by: Oren Shomron <shomron@apple.com>

58385c3fff60776f5dbeb2d920b5b6a1c4d016d5.message:
eval: overhaul core evaluation logic 🔧 (#27)

Refactor core evaluation logic to use a dedicated Swift function (evalBlock) for each block, whether it is part of the top-level Plan, BlockStmt, NotStmt or WithStmt.

Previously, block evaluation all happened in-line in evalFrame, and we had to manage our own stack and block/statement pointers manually. This led to several complications, including how to correctly handle BreakStmt and breaking out of several layers of blocks. Additionally, we conflated scopes (and sharing of locals or not) with the context in which each block executed, which led to more issues. Finally, propagation of undefined back up the call stack was confusing.

Now whenever we determine a block is undefined, we can simply return .undefined and handle its propagation at the caller. Additionally, we finally have correct break behavior, which is managed by returning a breakCounter to each caller which they then inspect and respond to.

Compliance tests passing are up from ✅ 771->991 📈

Signed-off-by: Oren Shomron <shomron@apple.com>
